title: The Educated Barbarian: Book of Five Rings analysis (part. 9)
summary: Final episode of NH's reading of Musashi's Book of Five Rings, covering the end of the Book of the Wind (speed vs rhythm, sparing effort, not appearing busy, pointing out the gate) and the Book of the Void. He links rhythm and sustainable effort to training, critiques workplace theater and modern teaching, and frames the void as a personal 'true way' each person must find, with teachers only providing keys.

claims.claim: Musashi says speed is not part of the true way; NH reads it as speed being a quality of rhythm, and a master appears effortless rather than fast.

In training, there is no point giving everything for one day then being out for seven; someone who trains every day while managing recovery, volume and intensity wins because he accumulates more tonnage.
Training once a week all-out means 4 sessions a month; someone training 4 times a week objectively beats you on tonnage and volume however hard you think you went.
Like the most explosive predators that go all-out for a few minutes a day, lifters should pick their efforts; hard sets are the exception, not the norm.
His channel only shows his 100% working sets, which can mislead viewers; warm-ups make up most of his training time.
Don't deliberately slow down or speed up; work at your own rhythm, matched to the goal, like a sprinter versus a 10k runner.
Time management is a key life skill: undershooting wastes time, overshooting forces you to drop tasks and damages long-term planning.
Western (and Japanese) workplaces reward looking busy over results; NH has experienced being a high performer penalized for not putting on that theater.
You cannot be a one-speed person; you must shift gears to adapt to your environment.
He prefers Musashi's teaching style of 'don't do that' over spoon-feeding answers; modern teaching is downloading knowledge to regurgitate rather than learning to find one's own path.
On his channel he will give keys of understanding but never feed the answer, because a found answer is worth more.

Many lifting beginners need to be reassured with promised results; fitness influencers 'point out the gate' as an easy, enticing way to teach, which creates cookie-cutter followers and supplement-pushing false promises.
Keep your spirit true: standing up for what you believe takes courage, but once you do, no bullying or dishonesty can move you.
The Book of the Void is not nihilism; NH reads it as the way existing in everything, reached when doubt no longer clouds your direction.
Deciding your life's direction already puts you ahead even if it changes; the way is subjective and changes with you.
No one can bring you to enlightenment; those claiming to do so usually lie for profit or ego, but keys can be passed on.
Beyond lifting, he preaches whatever physical activity makes you happy.
